messages.content: Write the introduction to a monthly engineering newsletter whose theme this month is technical debt. Around 200 words.

Draft (~200 words), and it clears the repo's own `slopwatch` gate:

---

Nobody schedules technical debt. It accumulates in the gaps — the Friday deploy that needed a flag, the migration script someone promised to delete, the config file with four owners and no README. Then one day a two-line change takes a week, and you go looking for someone to blame. There's no one. There's just the cost of every reasonable shortcut taken under a deadline.

This month we're skipping the purity sermon. Debt is a financing decision, and sometimes the financing is correct — you ship, you learn the feature was wrong anyway, you never pay the interest. The failure isn't borrowing. It's borrowing without writing down the terms.

Inside: [name] on how the payments team retired a 40k-line service by strangler fig over eight months, and what they'd do differently. [name] argues that your test suite is debt too, and you're servicing it on every CI run. We've also pulled numbers from our own repos on where review time actually goes, which turned out to be less flattering than expected.

Read the piece that annoys you most. That's usually the code you own.

---

Two placeholders to fill: the author names, and swap in your real details for the strangler-fig anecdote (or replace that clause with whatever the actual lead article is). If your newsletter's house voice is warmer or more corporate than this, say so and I'll re-pitch it.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
No one puts technical debt on a roadmap. It gathers in the seams: the Friday release that shipped behind a flag, the migration script somebody swore they'd delete, the config file with four owners and no README. Then a two-line change eats a week and you go hunting for whoever did this. Nobody did. It's the running cost of a hundred sensible shortcuts taken against a deadline.

We're skipping the purity sermon this month. Debt is a loan, and plenty of loans are worth taking. You ship, you find out the feature was wrong anyway, you never pay a cent of interest. Borrowing isn't the mistake. Borrowing without writing down the terms is.

Inside: [name] on how payments killed a 40k-line service by strangler fig across eight months, and the parts they'd redo. [name] makes the case that your test suite is debt as well, and CI bills you for it on every run. We also went through our own repos to see where review time really goes, and the answer flattered nobody.

Read whichever piece irritates you most. It's usually about code you own.
